name: Amaralingeswara Swamy Temple, Amaravati
deity: Shiva, worshipped as Amareswara (Amaralingeswara); consort Bala Chamundika
period: Eastern Chalukya; standing temple 11th century CE (earliest inscription 1129 CE)
dynasty: Eastern Chalukya (later Reddi, Vijayanagara and Vasireddy patronage)
summary: On the south bank of the Krishna at Amaravati, Shiva rises as a towering white linga worshipped from an upper storey — the Amaralingeswara temple, one of the five Pancharama Kshetras and the dwelling place of the immortals.

sections.history: Amaravati's Amaralingeswara temple crowns the low hill of Krouncha Saila on the south bank of the Krishna, in a town whose great Buddhist stupa once made it a Satavahana capital. The standing temple belongs to the eleventh century, and its earliest inscription is dated 1129 CE, though tradition and the Pancharama legend reach far deeper into antiquity. Raised under the Eastern Chalukyas, it was enriched across the centuries by the Reddi kings, the emperors of Vijayanagara, and later the Vasireddy family of Amaravati, whose zamindar Vasireddy Venkatadri Nayudu is remembered for restoring and endowing the shrine. Some thirty-five stone inscriptions in Telugu and Sanskrit are set into its walls, a running archive of the gifts and repairs that kept the temple alive through changing dynasties. It remains a living centre of worship and one of the five Pancharama Kshetras that bind the temples of coastal Andhra into a single sacred geography.
sections.architecture: The temple's marvel is its central linga — a slender white shaft rising about fifteen feet (4.5 m), so tall that priests perform worship from a raised upper platform built around it at first-floor height, an arrangement found in few temples anywhere. Local devotion holds that the linga once kept growing skyward until a nail was driven into its crown to still it, and a mark is pointed out as the spot. Four gopurams open the enclosure around a central vimana over the sanctum, and the whole carries the Dravidian idiom of the Eastern Chalukyas blended with Chola sensibility. The upper storey gathers a cluster of shrines — Kala Bhairava, guardian of the kshetra, alongside Mallikarjuna and Kashi Vishweswara — so that a circuit of the temple becomes a small pilgrimage in itself. The consort Bala Chamundika is enshrined as the presiding goddess.
sections.legends: The Pancharama story begins with the asura Tarakasura, made invincible by a Shiva linga he wore at his throat. When Kartikeya faced him in battle the demon could not fall until Vishnu revealed the secret; the boy-god shattered the linga with the fire-weapon, and its five pieces, humming 'Om' as they sought to rejoin, were fixed where they fell and temples raised above them. Amaravati holds one of these five. An older tradition tells that Indra, king of the gods, himself installed and worshipped the linga here; because the devas — the amara, the immortals — came to dwell in this place, it took the name Amaravati, the city of the immortals, and its lord became Amareswara.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the great festival of Amaralingeswara, when night-long worship and vast crowds fill the hill above the Krishna. The temple also keeps Navaratri for the goddess Bala Chamundika, the Kartika Purnima with its river-lit lamps, and the annual Kalyanotsavam celebrating the divine marriage of Shiva and his consort. A Rathayatra draws the deities through the town in procession. On these days the usual hours extend well into the night to receive the pilgrims.
sections.experience: To visit Amaravati is to stand where the sacred and the ancient overlap — the temple shares its riverside town with one of India's greatest Buddhist stupas and, today, with a new state capital rising nearby. Leave your footwear at the threshold and climb to the upper platform to meet the towering linga face to face, a perspective the raised worship makes unusually intimate. Pause at the guardian Kala Bhairava and the upper shrines, then step out to the ghats where the Krishna slides past. Mornings are cool and unhurried; the river breeze and the white gopurams make the hill a quietly memorable stop on the Pancharama trail.

visit.timings: Open daily from about 6:00 am to 12:30 pm and again from 4:00 pm to 8:30 pm; on Maha Shivaratri and other major festival days the hours extend late into the night.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — sarees or salwar for women, dhoti or shirt and trousers for men; footwear is left outside the temple before entering.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer courtyards but not inside the inner sanctum; watch for posted signs and follow the priests' guidance near the shrine.
visit.gettingThere: The nearest hub is Vijayawada, about 30–35 km away, with Vijayawada airport (VGA) and Vijayawada Junction railway station; APSRTC buses run to Amaravati from Vijayawada, Guntur and Mangalagiri, and the town is an easy road trip from either city.
